text: As of end-June 2025, Singapore's population was 6.11 million, comprising 4.20 million residents—3.66 million citizens and 540,000 permanent residents—and 1.91 million non-residents. The country is a multi-racial, multi-ethnic, and multi-cultural society, broadly classified under the CMIO system: Chinese, Malay, Indian, and Other. While Malays are recognised as the indigenous community, 75.5 percent of citizens and permanent residents are ethnic Chinese, with Malays and Indians making up 15.1 and 7.6 percent respectively. These three groups account for 98.2 percent of the ethnic citizen population, with the remaining 1.8 percent classified as Other, largely Eurasians. Major religions include Buddhism, Christianity, Islam, Taoism, and Hinduism. Non-residents, whose numbers have risen sharply since the 1990s and accounted for nearly 30 percent of the total population in 2020, are excluded from resident statistics and may originate from nationalities beyond the CMIO framework. Officially, mixed-race Singaporeans are typically assigned their father's race, though their identity card may also reflect both parents' ethnicities. Singapore has four official languages: English, Malay, Mandarin, and Tamil, with Malay designated as the national language and English as the main working language. The education system is bilingual, requiring English as the medium of instruction and a second language—usually Malay, Mandarin, or Tamil. Singlish, a local creole, is commonly spoken in informal settings across all major ethnic groups. In 2024, the resident total fertility rate (TFR) was 0.97, with Chinese at 0.83, Malays at 1.58, and Indians at 0.91; Singapore had one of the world's eight lowest TFRs in 2023. Population growth in Singapore was driven by immigration from the time Stamford Raffles landed in 1819, when the population was estimated at around 1,000. The first official census in January 1824 recorded 10,683 residents: 4,580 Malays, 3,317 Chinese, 1,925 Bugis, 756 Indians, 74 Europeans, 16 Armenians, and 15 Arabs. Chinese males greatly outnumbered females in 1826—5,747 males versus 341 females—compared to 2,501 Malay males and 2,289 females. Indian males also outnumbered females, with 209 male and 35 female Bengalis, and 772 males and 5 females from the Coromandel Coast. By 1836, the population reached 29,980, with Chinese making up 45.9% and Malays 41.9%, marking the first time Malays were outnumbered. Women from China were discouraged from emigrating, and most Chinese females were likely nyonyas from Malacca; by 1837, there were no Chinese women who had emigrated directly from China. The sex imbalance continued, with 130,367 Chinese males and 33,674 females in 1901. This imbalance meant fewer births in early Singapore, and by the late 1890s, only about 10% of the Chinese population were born in Singapore. Many early migrant workers from China and India did not intend to settle permanently, working to send remittances home and returning after earning money. From the 1920s, more Chinese chose to settle permanently, especially as conditions in Singapore became more favourable. Changing social attitudes allowed Chinese women to emigrate from China, leading to a gradual normalisation of the sex ratio and an increase in native births. Immigration remained the primary driver of Chinese population growth until 1931–1947, when natural increase surpassed net immigration. After World War II, from 1947 to 1957, population growth was driven by increased native births, with the birth rate peaking at 42.7 per thousand in 1957—the same year the United States saw its peak birth rate. Immigration declined sharply after Singapore's independence due to tighter controls from Malaysia and other countries. From 1970 to 1980, natural increase accounted for 315,400 population growth compared to only 24,000 from net migration. However, due to a low natural growth rate and labour demands, the government shifted policy in the 1980–1990 period to allow more foreigners, increasing net migration to nearly 200,000. By 1990–2000, net migration of over 600,000 surpassed natural growth and accounted for nearly two-thirds of population increase, with 664,083 recorded in the 1990–2000 decade. Due to low birth rates, the government adjusted immigration policies over time. Since the 2000s and 2010s, foreign talent with professional qualifications and less-skilled foreign workers have made up a significant and growing portion of the population. Curbs on immigration began in the 2010s to address rising social issues. Post-war birth booms led to family planning initiatives; by 1960, the government publicly funded such programmes. After independence in 1965, the birth rate fell to 29.5 per thousand and the natural growth rate to 2.5%, with an average of one baby born every 11 minutes in 1965. Kandang Kerbau Hospital (KKH), which specialised in women's health, delivered over 100 babies per day in 1962 and 39,835 in 1966, earning a place in the Guinness Book of World Records for ten years. Mothers with routine deliveries were discharged within 24 hours due to bed shortages. In September 1965, Minister for Health Yong Nyuk Lin submitted a white paper recommending a "Five-year Mass Family Planning programme" to reduce the birth rate to 20.0 per thousand by 1970. The Family Planning and Population Board (FPPB) was established in 1966 to provide clinical services and public education. By 1970, the Stop at Two campaign was established, using incentives, disincentives, and public exhortation to discourage families from having more than two children. After 1975, the fertility rate declined below replacement level, indicating demographic transition. In 1983, the Graduate Mothers' Scheme was introduced to encourage educated women, especially university graduates, to marry and have children, while discouraging women without O-level qualifications from having children—sparking the Great Marriage Debate. In 1986, the government reversed its policy—except for low-income, low-education women—and launched the Have Three or More (if you can afford it) campaign, offering cash and administrative incentives. In 2001, the Baby Bonus scheme was introduced. Singapore has one of the world's lowest fertility rates; in 2012, the TFR was 1.20, a sub-replacement rate. In 2004, Chinese TFR was 1.07 (1.65 in 1990), Malay TFR was 2.10 (2.69 in 1990), and Indian TFR was 1.30 (1.89 in 1990)—all declining further by 2006. The elderly (65 and above) made up 9.9% of the population in 2012, still lower than in many developed nations like the United States and Japan. In February 2015, the National University of Singapore launched the "New Age Institute" with Washington University in St. Louis to research ageing and fertility. Singapore's population is generally housed in new towns—large-scale, self-contained satellite developments with public housing, private housing, town centres, and amenities. Since the 1950s, Singapore had a city centre surrounded by slums and squatter colonies. By 1959, housing shortages and rapid population growth led to congestion and squalor. The new towns concept was introduced in July 1952 by the Housing and Development Board (HDB) to address housing shortages and relocate people from the city centre. Today, there are 23 new towns and 3 estates, with Bedok being the largest by area and population. In early 2013, Parliament debated the Population White Paper (PWP) titled A Sustainable Population for a Dynamic Singapore, which projected that by 2030, around 900,000 baby boomers would make up one quarter of the citizen population and that the workforce would shrink from 2020 onwards. The paper projected a total population between 6.5 and 6.9 million, with residents between 4.2 and 4.4 million and citizens between 3.6 and 3.8 million. It recommended increasing foreign workers to balance skilled and less-skilled labour and to support healthcare and domestic services, noting that foreign workers help businesses during economic growth. The motion passed 77 to 13 in the PAP-dominated Parliament after amendments that removed "population policy" and emphasized infrastructure and transport. Opposition came from non-PAP members, including all seven Workers' Party (WP) MPs and three Non-constituency Members of Parliament (NCMPs)—two from WP and one from Singapore People's Party (SPP)—as well as several Nominated Members of Parliament. Outside Parliament, the PWP was heavily criticised by opposition parties and critics. WP's Low Thia Khiang argued that increasing fertility would raise living costs and discourage young couples from having children, and that immigrants create friction and strain on infrastructure. On 16 February 2013, an estimated 4,000 Singaporeans gathered at Speakers' Corner in Hong Lim Park to protest the PWP, expressing concerns about strained public services and rising living costs—this was the largest anti-government protest at the venue since 2000. The CMIO framework was first proposed in 1956 during British colonial rule to structure the education system around four national languages. After independence in 1965, population growth was dominated by native births. Net immigration fell to 24,000 in the 1970–1980 period due to tighter controls. Fertility among Chinese declined sharply after the post-war boom, while Malay fertility remained relatively high, leading to a rise in the Malay share of the population to 14.5% in the late-1960s. From the 1980s, immigration policy shifted, leading to a sharp increase in immigrants. From 1990 to 2000, immigration overtook natural growth, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the decadal increase with 640,571 net migrants. The racial composition of citizens has remained relatively stable, though the proportion of Malays among residents declined slightly, while the proportion of Indian residents rose to 9.2% in 2010, up from 7.4% among citizens alone, due to increased migrant workers from South Asia, especially in construction. The population profile changed significantly after the 1980s relaxation of immigration policy, with a sharp rise in transient foreigners. Official figures show non-residents grew from 30,900 in 1970 to 1,641,600 in 2020—a 53-fold increase—representing 2.9% in 1970 and 28.9% in 2020. No detailed breakdown of non-residents by ethnic origin is publicly available, and it is widely assumed they come from a broad range of countries outside the CMIO framework. By the mid-2020s, it was estimated that over 40% of Singapore's total population were of foreign origin, including both permanent residents and non-residents, such as foreign workers, students, and their dependants. When Raffles arrived in January 1819, Singapore had approximately 120 Malays, 30 Chinese, and some native tribes (Orang Laut) under the Temenggung, with around 100 Malays having moved from Johor in 1811. Other estimates place the population at 1,000, belonging to various local tribes. Early census data show a long influx of migrant workers, initially mostly Malays, followed by others.

Singapore, established as a British free port by Stamford Raffles in the 19th century, initially had a small native population dominated by three main immigrant groups. When Raffles arrived in January 1819, Singapore had about 120 Malays, 30 Chinese, and some Orang Laut under the Temenggung, with around 100 Malays having migrated from mainland Johor in 1811. Some estimates suggest the population was as high as 1,000 belonging to various local tribes. By 1821, the population had grown to 4,724 Malays and 1,150 Chinese. In the 1824 census, 6,505 out of 10,683 people were Malays and Bugis, making up over 60% of the population. Chinese migrants, mostly male, began arriving shortly after the British settlement, and by 1826, the total population was 13,750, including 6,088 Chinese, 4,790 Malays, 1,242 Bugis, 1,021 Indians (244 from Bengal and 777 from the Coromandel Coast), 267 Javanese, 87 Europeans, and others. The population reached 16,000 in 1829 and 26,000 by 1834. By 1836, the Chinese population of 13,749 became the largest ethnic group, surpassing the Malay group (12,538, which included Bugis, Javanese, and Balinese). By 1849, the population had grown to 59,043, with 24,790 being Chinese. Many Chinese migrants in the 19th century worked on pepper and gambier plantations, with 11,000 recorded in one year. Singapore became a major entry and dispersal point for Chinese and Indian migrants working in plantations and mines in the Straits Settlements, many of whom settled in Singapore after their contracts ended. By 1860, the total population was around 90,000, of which 50,000 were Chinese and 2,445 were Europeans and Eurasians. The first comprehensive census was conducted in 1871, with people categorized into 33 racial, ethnic, or national groups, and Chinese making up 57.6%. Censuses followed every decade thereafter. In 1881, people were grouped into six main categories and further divided into 47 sub-categories. In 1921, the six broad groups were Europeans, Eurasians, Malays, Chinese, Indians, and Others. The Malays group included natives of the Malay archipelago, Europeans included Americans, and Indians encompassed people from the Indian subcontinent, including present-day Pakistan and Bangladesh. In 1901, the total population was 228,555, with 15.8% Malays, 71.8% Chinese, 7.8% Indians, and 3.5% Europeans and Eurasians. The Chinese population remained above 70% of the total, reaching 77.8% in 1947. The Malay population stabilized between 11% and 16% in the first half of the 20th century, while Indians ranged between 7% and just over 9%. Singapore has four official languages: English, Malay, Mandarin, and Tamil. Malay is the national language, though English is the official language of education and government. The colloquial English-based creole, known as Singlish, is widely spoken by all racial groups. The government promotes Mandarin, while the use of other Chinese dialects such as Hokkien, Teochew, Cantonese, and Hakka has declined over the past two decades, though they are still used by older generations. About 60% of Indian Singaporeans are Tamils, though only 37% speak Tamil at home according to the 2010 census; other Indian languages include Punjabi, Malayalam, Hindi, and Bengali, none of which is spoken by more than 10% of Indian Singaporeans. A large proportion of Indian Singaporeans also speak English at home. Around 5,000 to 10,000 Peranakans, descendants of early Chinese settlers, still use the Hokkien-influenced Malay dialect known as Baba Malay. The main religions in Singapore are Chinese folk religion, Buddhism, Taoism, Confucianism, Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, and Sikhism, with a significant number of people professing no religion. Singapore is a secular state with freedom of religion, though the government restricts certain religions like Jehovah’s Witnesses due to opposition to conscription. Most Malays are Muslim, while the majority of Chinese practice Buddhism and syncretic Chinese folk traditions; Christianity is growing. Taoism was overtaken as the second-most prominent religion among Chinese in the 2000 census, as more identified as Buddhists than Taoists. Indians are mostly Hindu, though many are Muslim, Sikh, or Christian. People with no religion form the second-largest group. Among residents aged 25–39, the percentage of university graduates rose from 23.7% in 2001 to 45.9% in 2011, while those with a diploma or professional qualification increased from 15.9% to 22.9% over the same period. In 2005, the unemployment rate for persons aged 15 and over was 2.5%, the lowest in four years, with a labour force of 2.3 million. The average household monthly income was SGD 4,943 in 2000, an increase of SGD 3,080 from 1990 at an average annual rate of 4.9%. In 1999, income dropped 2.7% due to an economic slowdown, measured in 1990 dollars, the average income rose from SGD 3,080 in 1990 to SGD 4,170 in 2000 at an average annual rate of 3.1%. After recovering from the 1998 economic slowdown, household income growth resumed in 2000, but for the lowest two deciles, income declined compared to 1999, primarily due to the proportion of households with no income earner rising from 75% in 1999 to 87% in 2000, including retired elderly and unemployed members. Income disparity widened in 2000, reflecting faster growth among higher-income households.
